sections.normalized_html:
Recall that a matrix [MATH: A] is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix [MATH: P] such that

[MATH: A=PDP^T,] where [MATH: D] is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

[MATH: D=P^TAP.]

Moreover, a matrix [MATH: A] is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that [MATH: A] is symmetric and [MATH: D] is diagonal. Therefore, [MATH: D=P^T \! AP] gives an orthogonal diagonalization of [MATH: A.]

From the diagonal matrix [MATH: D] we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix [MATH: A] are [MATH: \lambda_1=-1] and [MATH: \lambda_2=1.] So, the first column of [MATH: P] corresponds to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_1=-1.]

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to [MATH: \lambda_1=-1.] Computing [MATH: A-(-1)I,] we get

[MATH: A + I|= [0|− 1; − 1|0] + [1|0; 0|1]; = [1|− 1; − 1|1].]

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix [MATH: M] which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

[MATH: M|= [1|− 1|0; − 1|1|0]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + R_{1}; ∼[1|− 1|0; 0|0|0]]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the [MATH: 1]st one). Thus, [MATH: x_2] is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain [MATH: x_1=x_2.] Hence, the general solution is

[MATH: [x_{2}; x_{2}]]

Therefore, setting [MATH: x_2=1,] we get the eigenvector

[MATH: [1; 1]]

where [MATH: \| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2}.] Dividing [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] by its norm, we obtain the first column of [MATH: P\mathbin{:}] [MATH: [1; 1]]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A square matrix [MATH: A] is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix [MATH: P] such that

Content:
[MATH: A=PDP^T,]
where [MATH: D] is a diagonal matrix. Note that this is equivalent to the equation

Content:
[MATH: D = P^TAP.]

Content:
So, to orthogonally diagonalize a matrix [MATH: A,] we need to find a diagonal matrix [MATH: D] and an orthogonal matrix [MATH: P] that satisfies the above equations.

Content:
A helpful theorem allows us to determine whether a real matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable. It states the following:

Content:
> A matrix [MATH: A] with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Content:
Consequently, every symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable!

Content:
For example, the symmetric matrix

Content:
[MATH: [3|3; 3|− 5]]

Content:
has the orthogonal diagonalization

Content:
[MATH: A|= [(3)/(sqrt(10))|(1)/(sqrt(10)); (1)/(sqrt(10))|− (3)/(sqrt(10))]_(⏟)_(P)[4|0; 0|− 6]_(⏟)_(D)[(3)/(sqrt(10))|(1)/(sqrt(10)); (1)/(sqrt(10))|− (3)/(sqrt(10))]^{T}_(⏟)_(P^{T}),]

Content:
where [MATH: P] is orthogonal, and [MATH: D] is diagonal. As usual, the entries on the main diagonal of [MATH: D] are the eigenvalues of [MATH: A.] Also, the columns of [MATH: P] are orthonormal eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalues of [MATH: A.]

Content:
The procedure of the orthogonal diagonalization of a [MATH: 2 \times 2] real symmetric matrix [MATH: A] is almost the same as the diagonalization of a matrix:

Content:
- Step 1: Find the eigenvalues of the matrix [MATH: A].
- Step 2: Find a basis of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] consisting of unit orthogonal eigenvectors of [MATH: A.]
- Step 3: Construct the matrices [MATH: D] and [MATH: P.]

Content:
In the case of symmetric matrices, the two eigenvectors we compute in step 2 will always be orthogonal, provided that they correspond to different eigenvalues. However, we must also ensure that we normalize those eigenvectors.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Parts of an Orthogonal Diagonalization

Example Prompt:
[MATH: [∗|− (sqrt(10))/(10); ∗|− (3sqrt(10))/(10)]]
Consider the matrix [MATH: P] shown above. Given that [MATH: A=PDP^T] is an orthogonal diagonalization of a [MATH: 2\times 2] symmetric matrix [MATH: A] for some diagonal matrix [MATH: D,] which of the following could be the first column of the matrix [MATH: P?]

[MATH: [(3sqrt(10))/(10); − (sqrt(10))/(10)]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that a matrix [MATH: A] is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix [MATH: P] such that

[MATH: A=PDP^T,]
where [MATH: D] is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix [MATH: A] is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since [MATH: A=PDP^T] is an orthogonal diagonalization of a [MATH: 2\times 2] symmetric matrix [MATH: A,] the matrix [MATH: P] must be a [MATH: 2\times 2] orthogonal matrix. This means that

- the first column must be orthogonal to the second column, and
- the norm of the first column must be equal to [MATH: 1.]

Among the given options, only the vector [MATH: [(3sqrt(10))/(10); − (sqrt(10))/(10)]] has both properties.

Item 5 — Example: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 2x2 Symmetric Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization

Example Prompt:
[MATH: [0|− 1; − 1|0]]
Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that [MATH: D=P^T \! AP,] where [MATH: P] is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first column of the matrix [MATH: P?]

[MATH: [(sqrt(2))/(2); (sqrt(2))/(2)]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that a matrix [MATH: A] is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix [MATH: P] such that

[MATH: A=PDP^T,]
where [MATH: D] is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

[MATH: D=P^TAP.]

Moreover, a matrix [MATH: A] is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that [MATH: A] is symmetric and [MATH: D] is diagonal. Therefore, [MATH: D=P^T \! AP] gives an orthogonal diagonalization of [MATH: A.]

From the diagonal matrix [MATH: D] we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix [MATH: A] are [MATH: \lambda_1=-1] and [MATH: \lambda_2=1.] So, the first column of [MATH: P] corresponds to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_1=-1.]

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to [MATH: \lambda_1=-1.] Computing [MATH: A-(-1)I,] we get

[MATH: A + I|= [0|− 1; − 1|0] + [1|0; 0|1]; = [1|− 1; − 1|1].]

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix [MATH: M] which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

[MATH: M|= [1|− 1|0; − 1|1|0]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + R_{1}; ∼[1|− 1|0; 0|0|0]]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the [MATH: 1]st one). Thus, [MATH: x_2] is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain [MATH: x_1=x_2.] Hence, the general solution is

[MATH: [x_{2}; x_{2}]]

Therefore, setting [MATH: x_2=1,] we get the eigenvector

[MATH: [1; 1]]

where [MATH: \| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2}.] Dividing [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] by its norm, we obtain the first column of [MATH: P\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: [1; 1]]
